newsitem.title: USA: U.S. proposes inspections for biological weapons.
newsitem.headline: U.S. proposes inspections for biological weapons.

text.p: The United States, saying that the number of nations holding or seeking germ warfare agents has doubled since a treaty banning them went into force, called on Monday for an inspection system to be set up.

John Holum, director of the Arms Control and Disarmament Agency, said that partly because of a boom in biotechnology, there was a mounting threat from "tyrants and terrorists who would return us to the Dark Ages" by developing biological weapons.

Holum's speech to a conference that opened on Monday in Geneva will be delivered on Tuesday, but it was released in advance by the U.S. arms-control agency in Washington. The conference of 138 countries is reviewing the two-decade-old Biological Weapons Convention.

"Overall, the United States believes that twice as many countries now have or are actively pursuing offensive biological weapons capabilities as when the Convention went into force (in 1975)," Holum said.
The only countries he named were the already-known cases of Russia -- which has renounced germ warfare -- and Iraq.

Growth in the science of biotechnology is benefiting mankind in the fields of health, agriculture and protection of the environment but is also creating "a burgeoning global (biological-warfare) potential," Holum said.
He noted that the era of biological warfare began when the bodies of Tatar soldiers who had died of the plague were thrown over the walls of the besieged city of Kaffa in the Crimea in 1346.

"Now we face tyrants and terrorists who would return us to the Dark Ages. Today's outlaws share their predecessors' ancient depravity. But the means at their disposal are frighteningly modern," Holum said.
"We can wait for tragedy -- for biological weapons to surpass what other weapons have done in Tokyo, Oklahoma City or the Gulf War ... Or we can act."

A Japanese cult is accused of releasing nerve gas in the Tokyo subway in March 1995, killing 12 people. The bombing of a federal building in Oklahoma City a month later killed 168. Continuing controversy surrounds the accidental exposure of U.S. troops to Iraqi nerve gas in the 1991 Gulf War.
Because the biological convention was drawn up in the Cold War era, it lacked a provision for on-site inspections, as in more recent arms pacts. But a group of experts is working to remedy that.
Holum said the provision should be completed by 1998, not 2001 as the group intends. He called the later deadline "inappropriately relaxed."
He said the protocol should provide for "investigations in all cases presenting credible evidence of (biological weapon) development or production."
Western diplomats say non-aligned countries do not view the biological-weapons issue as a priority and oppose intrusive inspection measures.
